title: How EPI-CATCH is teaching plants new tricks
content:
Plants have no brain, no nerves, and no ability to move away from danger. However, they can remember droughts, heatwaves, salinity, and other environmental stresses, and, in some cases, even pass those memories on to their offspring. Understanding how they do this was at the heart of the COST Action Epigenetic mechanisms of crop adaptation to climate change (EPI-CATCH).

The COST Action EPI-CATCH aimed to shed light on one of the most intriguing of these mechanisms: epigenetics. These biological processes enable plants to adjust to their environment without altering their DNA sequence. Over the course of four years, the Action brought together researchers from over 30 countries, trained a new generation of scientists, and produced knowledge that could help to develop climate-resilient crops for the future.

“We wanted to define, develop, and share new knowledge and methodologies for investigating epigenetic mechanisms involved in plant adaptation to environmental stresses driven by climate change,” says Prof. Federico Martinelli of the University of Florence, the Action Chair.

Did you know?

Some studies show that plants pass on epigenetic information better than animals

title: Showing up for Public Data: Our Gratitude
content:
For many of us, the Data Rescue Project was a lifeline over the past two years, giving us space and agency to work towards the future we wanted to see happen. This November, as many in America are preparing to celebrate Thanksgiving, we are grateful to every one of you for showing up. Truly. We've said it before, and we've said it again: the DRP community gave us hope during some of our darkest moments.

The recent blue wave in the US Midterms also bolsters us– it exceeded expectations and predictions, affirming that the voting public is unhappy with current elected officials and looking for change. However, that doesn't mean our work is done. Nearly all federal data is created under the executive branch, which has not changed hands. Federal data continues to be threatened, both in the short and long terms, so we need to continue showing up. 

We must carry on rescuing data and monitoring changes to these valuable resources. We have the responsibility to advocate for access to public data and build awareness among our community and users. And not least of all, we need to document the damage done for accountability and plan for a brighter and more sustainable future for federal data.

title: ICE Out of NJ Demands Freedom for Junior Marte & Other Former Delaney Hall Hunger Strikers
content:
Democracy Now! has obtained exclusive audio from inside Delaney Hall, the controversial immigrant detention center in Newark, New Jersey, operated by the for-profit prison company GEO Group. The audio was recorded over the summer during a labor and hunger strike organized by immigrant detainees. Junior Marte, an asylum seeker and father from Venezuela, was one of the organizers. He describes conditions inside the facility, including abusive treatment, medical neglect and prolonged legal limbo.

“We are here unjustly, wrongfully accused of being criminals. Yet immigration officials refuse to review our cases, because they know that we are all innocent people,” Marte says in the message.

The hunger and labor strike lasted for a month, with an estimated 300 detained immigrants participating in the protest. Jenny Garcia, campaign coordinator at the American Friends Service Committee of New Jersey, says that since the strikes, GEO Group and ICE have taken “every opportunity to retaliate against the strikers, the families visiting outside, and the protesters.”

title: ECHOLOT partners join AI campaign
content:
Two ECHOLOT partners have officially joined the ‘INNOVATE. PROTECT. EMPOWER: How cultural heritage can make Public AI a reality’ campaign, which was launched by the EU-funded European Heritage Hub at the end of September.

Read more about the INNOVATE.PROTECT.EMPOWER campaign.

The campaign, which is co-organised by Europeana (one of our ECHOLOT consortium partners), followed the publication of the European Heritage Hub’s policy paper entitled “Beyond adopter and supplier: putting cultural heritage at the heart of Europe’s Public AI ecosystem”. The paper highlights the cultural heritage sector’s role in the European Commission’s forthcoming AI strategy for the cultural and creative sectors, which is expected in 2027. The campaign translates its key messages into a call to action, inviting organisations and networks across Europe to endorse it.

ECHOLOT’s project coordinator, the Leibniz Information Centre for Science and Technology and University Library (TIB), has officially joined the campaign, thereby strengthening ECHOLOT’s presence alongside Europeana.

title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
content:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

title: Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home
content:
(Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch said today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file new cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and users.

“President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”

title: Quantum may be a bigger security risk than AI. Europe’s got a plan.
content:
BRUSSELS — As the world seeks a way through a wave of AI-powered cyberattacks and rogue agents, the next security threat already looms: quantum technology. 

With quantum computers set to break long-established protocols for securing digital information and communications in everything from messaging to banking services, their deployment in the next few years will spark a new security scramble.

The EU is hoping to get ahead of the risks with a Quantum Act rolling out Wednesday, which aims to secure the bloc’s digital infrastructure, according to a draft obtained by POLITICO.

Even as AI has helped to disrupt services from supermarket fridges to the European Commission’s own platforms over the past month, computer scientists contend that another, potentially more perilous moment for cybersecurity is on the horizon: Q-Day.

The fear is that quantum computers, which can process more than the classic 0s and 1s used by today’s machines, will eclipse current security vulnerabilities by breaking the standard methods of encryption that scramble information in order to lock it down — rendering everything from secure government systems to hospitals digitally defenseless.

title: Proteiiniomavaraisuus on kansallisen turvallisuuden kysymys – entiset kenraalit varoittavat EU:n ruokaturvan riskeistä
content:
Tänään julkaistu ympäristöjärjestö WePlanetin raportti tarkastelee ruoan ja rehun, erityisesti proteiinin, tuontiriippuvuutta EU:ssa ja siihen liittyviä geopoliittisia riskejä. Suomessa ja EU:ssa kehitetäänkin uusia menetelmiä, joilla proteiinia voidaan tuottaa.

Huoltovarmuuskeskus (HVK) totesi maaliskuussa 2026, että Suomen on vahvistettava omavaraisuuttaan kasviproteiinin tuotannossa. Luonnonvarakeskuksen selvityksiin perustuvan arvion mukaan Suomen proteiiniomavaraisuus on matalalla tasolla, mikä heikentää ruokajärjestelmän kriisinkestävyyttä.

Erityisen riippuvaista tuonnista on kotieläintuotanto, jossa tarvitaan runsaasti täydentävää valkuaisrehua. Pitkittyneessä kriisitilanteessa myös ihmisten ravinnoksi tarvittavasta proteiinista tulee pulaa, jos korvaaviin vaihtoehtoihin ei ole varauduttu.

Sama ongelma koskee koko Eurooppaa.

Raportin yhteydessä julkaistaan avoin kirje, jossa entiset kenraalit kehottavat EU:n päättäjiä suhtautumaan proteiinitarjonnan vakavien häiriöiden mahdollisuuteen turvallisuuspoliittisena kysymyksenä.

title: ATO 2026: Open Source Licensing 101
content:
In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. McCoy Smith, Chair of OSI’s License Committee, presented “Open Source Licensing 101.”

This essential session is a basic primer on what the Open Source Initiative is, the Open Source licenses they approve, and the broader categories those license fall into. Also included are tips for understanding the OSI license approval process and the Open Source Definition and Open Source AI Definition. An overview of some of the more prominent approved Open Source licenses was provided. Other related topics like best practices, available resources and other information for working best within Open Source was also provided.

title: UK Hacker Sentenced to Seven Years, Then Released
content:
British hacker Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced to seven years in prison on Monday for a series of cyberattacks targeting major international companies, but was released from custody the same day after the court took into account time he had already spent in detention.

Woolwich Crown Court initially imposed a nine-year sentence, reducing it by two years to reflect time Kurtaj had spent under a hospital order. He was subsequently released on license, meaning he remains subject to supervision and conditions.

Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group, pleaded guilty on November 16 to six offenses, including fraud, four violations of the Computer Misuse Act and illegally possessing a mobile phone in prison. Seven additional charges were left on file.

His attacks between 2020 and 2022 targeted companies including Uber, Revolut, telecommunications operators BT and EE, and Rockstar Games, the developer of the Grand Theft Auto franchise.

title: EU budget: Costa’s latest proposal fails to satisfy either side
content:
“I am convinced that this proposal is a good starting point for reaching a final agreement for three reasons. First, it is a budget that matches our ambitions. Second, it keeps national contributions within reasonable limits. Third, it includes a balanced basket of new own resources,” António Costa said.

The document is intended to break the deadlock among EU member states over the budget. The goal remains to reach an agreement before the end of 2026, allowing the necessary legislation to be adopted in 2027 and the new budget to take effect on January 1, 2028, according to the European Council.

Costa’s proposal has failed to meet the expectations of the so-called frugal countries — a group of net contributors to the EU budget that includes Germany, Austria, Sweden, Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands.

These countries are demanding significantly deeper spending cuts. They argue that the budget should focus more heavily on new priorities, above all defense and the competitiveness of the European economy, and devote less funding to traditional spending areas.

title: Surf's up, borders down
content: The ocean doesn't respect man-made borders, and the Curonian Spit – a 98-kilometre stretch between the coast of Lithuania and Russia's Kaliningrad region – is a perfect example. In the cold Baltic waters, surfers from both countries line up to catch the same waves, but they cannot cross from one side to the other. Between them lies a NATO-Russia border, along which Lithuania’s chief of defence recently suggested installing physical barriers to ensure continuous patrols. Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Baltic Sea has become increasingly militarised and a stage for national military exercises. NATO has reinforced its maritime presence with warships, aircraft, and naval drones, while Russia maintains its Baltic Fleet in Kaliningrad. For Dima, surfer and member of Nida Surf Club on the Lithuanian side, nature makes these divisions look absurd. Both countries have the “same wind, same waves, same nature,” he tells The European Correspondent. title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
content:
A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.

Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
content:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.

title: UN Womenin ja UNODC:n raportti: joka tunti viisi naista kuoli kumppaninsa tai lähisukulaisensa surmaamana vuonna 2025
content:
Kansainvälisen naisiin kohdistuvan väkivallan vastaisen päivän yhteydessä julkaistu vuoden 2026 katsaus naissurmiin, Femicide Brief 2026, osoittaa, että koti on edelleen naisille ja tytöille vaarallisin paikka. Tilanne ei ole juurikaan muuttunut vuosiin. Vuonna 2025 kaikista 78 000 naisiin ja tyttöihin kohdistuneesta sukupuoleen perustuvasta surmasta 60 prosenttia oli kumppanin tai perheenjäsenen tekemiä. Tämä tarkoittaa keskimäärin viittä surmattua naista tai tyttöä joka tunti – yhteensä 129:ää päivässä.

Naiset ja tytöt eivät ole turvassa naissurmilta missään päin maailmaa. Afrikassa kumppanin tai perheenjäsenen tekemien naisten ja tyttöjen surmien määrä suhteessa naisväestöön on korkein: 2,9 uhria 100 000 naista ja tyttöä kohden. Seuraavina tulevat Amerikka (1,4), Oseania (1,1), Aasia (0,6) ja Eurooppa (0,5).

”Olemme nähneet hälyttäviä tilastoja aivan liian pitkään”, sanoo UNODC:n pääjohtaja Monica Juma.

title: University of Michigan Mailer Promises Its Data Center Isn’t Really a Data Center
content:
Over the past month, the University of Michigan sent postcards and pamphlets to people in Michigan telling them its new data center is “NOT a commercial data center” and is, instead, a “research computing center.”

According to one of the postcards viewed by 404 Media, the University’s data center will “advance breakthrough research in medicine, clean energy, cybersecurity, and engineering,” and "accelerate discoveries like new drug therapies and cancer treatments that improve people’s lives.” The University's postcard also promised to create 300 “high-quality union jobs during development” and “preserve approximately 80% of the 124-acre property as green space.”

One of U of M’s mailers said the building will not operate as a commercial data center. “This facility will not support streaming, entertainment, social media, or e-commerce,” it said. It also said the facility will not “burden the local community with the cost of its energy or water use, drain resources from the local community or raise utility rates,” or “create smoke, odors, or significant noise.”

title: Egypt: Authorities must reverse decision to close Mada Masr and drop all charges against its editor in chief Lina Attalah
content:
Ahead of an appeal hearing on 25 November against the closure of Mada Masr and the conviction of its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah for operating a website without a license Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Sara Hashash, said:

“Egyptian authorities have an opportunity to change course and meet their international obligations by reversing this disgraceful decision to shut down Mada Masr. The latest escalation against Mada Masr is a chilling signal of the Egyptian authorities’ resolve to silence independent journalism and eradicate any critical reporting that challenges the official narrative or scrutinizes their human rights record or other conduct. Egyptian authorities must immediately end their brazen assault on press freedom, quash the closure order against Mada Masr– one of the few remaining lifelines for independent information about Egypt.

“The authorities should also drop all charges against Lina Attalah who faces trial in a separate case, on charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence, for which she could be sentenced to up to one year in prison.

title: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
content:
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to agree on a “pact” that – despite making no clear reference to fossil fuels or adaptation finance – had contained strong signals for oceans.

The “Antalya pact” took up much of the two weeks of negotiating time in Turkey, only to be rejected during the closing plenary by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable countries.

Several countries expressed their regret during the plenary that significant work on advancing ocean-climate action would be lost.

title: "Only Path Forward Is to Abolish": Outcry After Masked ICE Agents Arrest Family at Seattle Airport
content:
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson and other officials in the state have denounced the violent arrest of a father and daughter by ICE agents on Saturday as they were boarding a flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Video of the arrest shows masked plainclothes agents dragging a woman off the jetway as she screams for help. Both Alaska Airlines and the Port of Seattle said ICE carried out the operation without their knowledge. ICE said Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, originally from Mexico, was targeted for overstaying his tourist visa, and that his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, would be charged with assault for allegedly throwing hot coffee at an agent — although witnesses dispute that account.

“This is one of, unfortunately, many thousands of detentions that is happening not only in Washington state, but across the country,” says Josefina Mora-Cheung, director of organizing for the immigrant justice group La Resistencia. “The only path forward is to abolish ICE.”

title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
content:
Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app.

Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “Intelligent Screen Context,” while Apple refers to it as either “Onscreen Awareness” or “Visual Intelligence.”

title: Pakistani Prisoners Face Poor Access to Health Care
content:
When Pakistani senators visited the prototype Islamabad Model Jail on November 19 and inspected the healthcare facilities that would be available to prisoners, they called them “adequate.” But the conditions they observed on their curated tour are a far cry from the reality most prisoners experience in Pakistan’s justice system.

Human Rights Watch has documented structural and systemic problems in Pakistan’s jails and prisons that leave most inmates with little access to health care. Many inmates who fall ill in custody fail to receive prompt or decent care at all.

After two prisoners died in Peshawar Central Prison following alleged delays in medical treatment, a lawyer petitioned the Peshawar High Court asking that prisons across the province be required to record when prisoners request medical help and establish clear procedures for emergency hospital transfers.

title: Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person in History to Win in Two Different Sciences
content:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes.

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “Floating University” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

title: Snowden on steroids: AI agents in phones trigger surveillance fears
content:
AI agents are lurking in your phone, hoovering up your messages, pictures and emails in a privacy breach that “makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” privacy proponents are warning.

Privacy-preserving messaging app Signal has started blocking screenshots by default in an attempt to stop AI agents from reading people’s screens and capturing potentially sensitive data.

The makers behind Signal — which is considered the industry gold standard for confidential, encrypted messaging — warned that Google, Apple and Microsoft are integrating autonomous agents “deep” within their device operating systems, allowing the agents to bypass privacy safeguards in individual apps.

“The ability for billions of devices to permanently spy on their users makes the Edward Snowden revelations look like a joke,” Udbhav Tiwari, head of strategy and global affairs at Signal, told POLITICO, referring to the 2013 disclosures about mass U.S. government surveillance.

Tiwari warned that governments with a penchant for surveillance could ask tech firms for access to data gathered by AI agents, skipping the need to break end-to-end encryption or install malware on someone’s device.

title: European Parts Made in 2026 Found in Russian Drones
content:
European electronic components manufactured as recently as February 2026 have been found in Russian drones used against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, highlighting Russia's continued access to foreign technology despite years of Western sanctions.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office said investigators have identified more than 16,000 foreign-made components in Russian drones, missiles and other weapons — the highest figure reported by Ukrainian authorities to date.

“Based on inspections of incident sites, expert examinations and analysis of physical evidence, more than 16,000 foreign-made components have been identified so far,” the office told OCCRP and its partners, the Kyiv Independent, De Tijd and Paper Trail Media. 

“These components are used in drones, missiles and other weapons in service with the aggressor state [Russia] (…) and bear the markings of companies from over 30 countries,” it said.

Ukraine's military intelligence has published details of more than 6,300 foreign-made components found in Russian weapons on its War & Sanctions website.

title: Life on the Edge of War: Are Poland and South Korea Safe?
content:
From the perspective of someone living in South Korea and observing the reality firsthand, the similarities in how people in both countries perceive security are striking  On one hand, life proceeds under the shadow of geopolitical struggles. In Poland, it is the war in Ukraine; in South Korea, it is the threat posed by a neighbouring country with which no peace treaty has been signed.

On the other hand, both societies face unexpected threats occurring on their own streets. Recently, both countries have witnessed terrorist attacks on civilian populations. These had devastating effects on the sense of security across both nations.

However, on-the-ground interviews conducted with South Koreans specifically for FocusEurope.pl, show that they have much more in common with their Polish counterparts. They seem remarkably adept at adapting to persistent threats .

In Seoul, you can walk home late or catch a cab without worrying whether the trip will be safe. The same goes for leaving your phone at the table while going to the restroom. People don’t automatically assume that someone will rob or take advantage of them.

title: Field notes from a failed COP31
content: Friday evening, the official final day of the COP31 climate negotiations. Standing on a chair with a red noose around his neck, Malaysian activist Amalen Sathananthar shouts: “You are killing the future! Why don’t you just kill me now?” It took two additional days – almost 50 hours into overtime – for delegates to give up. The EU and others rejected the final draft because it left out the two words at the root of the climate crisis: fossil fuels. They disappeared under pressure from Saudi Arabia and the Arab Group, backed by a bloc of like-minded developing countries, opposed to any mention of fossil fuels or “top-down” targets. The text “does not begin to address the climate emergency we face,” said Irish minister Darragh O'Brien. “The EU cannot accept it.” His words were met with applause. What is now the longest COP on record, is the first since 2009 to end without an overarching agreement. But this may not be the worst possible outcome. “This collapse is better than a half-hearted final document would have been,” said Johan Rockstrom and Ottmar Edenhofer from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research. title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
content:
Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.
snippet: Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

title: What the ICJ’s landmark genocide finding could mean for the case against Israel in Gaza
content:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) last week ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority group.

The court found Myanmar breached its obligations under the United Nations genocide convention to prevent and punish genocide.

This ruling is not just important for the Rohingya and Myanmar. It may also have a significant legal impact on other genocide cases before the court – in particular, South Africa’s case alleging Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.

Four cases currently before the ICJ concern allegations of breaches of the genocide convention.

One was brought by Ukraine against Russia following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Another was brought by Nicaragua against Germany, regarding Germany’s support of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The third was brought by the Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwanda, which includes claims about Rwanda’s involvement in conflict in the Kivu provinces of the DRC.

The Myanmar ruling may have repercussions for all these cases.

However, the judgement will mostly affect the fourth genocide case before the court, the one brought by South Africa against Israel.

title: Ethiopia: Lethal artillery strikes on civilian neighbourhoods in Tigray’s Alamata city must be investigated as war crimes
content:
Artillery attacks by Ethiopia’s military and its allied Tigray Peace Forces (TPF) that killed dozens of civilians and injured many more in the city of Alamata in the northern region of Tigray, between 26 and 28 September, must be investigated as possible war crimes, Amnesty International said today.

The organization also found that forces affiliated to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), put civilians in harm’s way by establishing military bases in populated residential areas, including in several schools in Alamata, prior to the outbreak of renewed fighting in the region.

The Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF) and its TPF allies seized control of the strategic city of Alamata, a key supply hub for troops, food, and fuel, from the TPLF on 28 September.

title: Too Big to Fire? Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia; Questions Loom Over AI Boom & U.S.-China Relations
content:
Nvidia stock prices surged over 30% on Monday as the chip maker reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang had stepped down earlier in November amid reports he had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI boom, and the leadership turmoil had erased trillions in value from the U.S. stock market. President Donald Trump acknowledged he had encouraged the company’s board to bring Huang back.

“The fact that our markets are so over-indexed on the AI trade, that something like three-fourths of gains in the [S&P 500] this past year have been AI-related, is unsustainable,” says Aya Ibrahim, senior fellow for economic and national security at the AI Now Institute.

We also speak with organizer and researcher Tobita Chow, who says Huang’s “spy scandal” that led to his ouster is part of a larger effort by anti-China figures in the U.S. national security establishment to escalate tensions between the countries.

title: EU: Forced Labor Remedies Should Center on Workers
content:
(Brussels) – Companies that receive complaints of forced labor in their operations or supply chains should make sure affected workers have access to full and effective remedies, Human Rights Watch and a group of civil society organizations and trade unions said in a report released today. 

In the White Paper on Remediation of Forced Labour in the Private Economy, the organizations set out what appropriate and effective remedies look like for workers, and the concrete steps companies should take to deliver it.

“Forced labor does not end when a product is pulled from the shelves but only when workers who were trapped by debt, deceived, or threatened get their wages, documents, and dignity back,” said Hélène de Rengervé, senior advocate at Human Rights Watch. “Companies should remedy labor abuses in their supply chains and engage with workers from the start to define appropriate solutions.”

title: Merz to meet Pope Leo, Meloni in Rome
content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will meet Pope Leo XIV and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Monday, three officials familiar with the plans told POLITICO.

The visit to the Vatican, Merz’s first private audience with the pope, is set to focus on human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine, two of the officials said.

Merz also plans to meet Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s top diplomat, who in September used his U.N. General Assembly speech to call for an immediate ceasefire in Ukraine and a path to diplomacy.

A German government spokesperson declined to comment, saying the chancellor’s trips are announced on the Friday of the preceding week.

Merz, a Catholic, attended Leo’s inauguration in May 2025 but did not meet the pontiff in private. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul met Parolin at the Vatican in early October for talks that also covered AI, the war in Ukraine and Black Sea grain exports.

title: Mitä tapahtuu vanhoilla kaatopaikoilla, kun yhdyskuntajätteet muhivat maan kerroksissa? – Jätekukko kehitti mittausvälineen selvitystyöhön
content:
Kaatopaikoilla syntyy metaania vielä vuosikymmeniä sen jälkeen, kun jätteiden loppusijoittaminen on päättynyt. Karkeasti ajateltuna sekajätteeseen aikanaan heitetyt banaaninkuoret aiheuttavat edelleen päästöjä syvällä maan sisässä. Kaatopaikan hapettomissa olosuhteissa orgaaninen jäte hajoaa ja muodostaa muun muassa metaania ja hiilidioksidia sekä rikkivetyä.

Kuopion Heinälamminrinteen jätekeskuksessa kaasujen muodostumista ja talteenottoa on tutkittu osana KAJASTUS-hanketta. Hankkeessa kehitetään menetelmiä, joilla voidaan vähentää metaanipäästöjä, lisätä talteen saatavan kaatopaikkakaasun määrää ja parantaa suljettujen kaatopaikkojen seurantaa.

Suljettukin kaatopaikka elää

Orgaanisen jätteen sijoittamista kaatopaikoille rajoitettiin Suomessa merkittävästi vuonna 2016. Kuopion seudun sekajätteet sijoitettiin pääsääntöisesti kaatopaikalle ennen kuin Riikinvoiman ekovoimalaitos aloitti toimintansa samana vuonna.

Suljettu eli käytöstä poistettu kaatopaikka peitetään esimerkiksi savi- tai muovikerroksilla, jotka lähtökohtaisesti pitävät kaatopaikkakaasut kurissa. Jätemassan painuminen ja liikkuminen voi kuitenkin synnyttää vuotoja etenkin kaivojen, putkien ja muiden läpivientien kohdalle.

title: Landmines: New Use, Production Undermine Ban Treaty
content:
(Geneva, November 24, 2026) – New use, production, and acquisition of antipersonnel landmines contributed to killing or injuring at least 6,929 people in 2025, which is the highest annual total since 2020, Human Rights Watch said today with the release of the “Landmine Monitor 2026” by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the campaign and contributed to the report.

The 200-page report examines global compliance with the 1997 Mine Ban Treaty and the challenges facing the treaty nearly three decades after its adoption. The treaty comprehensively bans antipersonnel mines and commits countries to eliminate stockpiled weapons, clear contaminated land, and assist mine victims and affected communities.

“At a time when civilian casualties are rising and new technologies make mines easier to deploy, supporting the Mine Ban Treaty is more important than ever,” said Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “All countries should join the treaty, and members should fully uphold its obligations.”

title: Right-wing revolt threatens to bog down EU budget
content:
BRUSSELS — The far-right Patriots for Europe group plans to challenge the European Parliament’s negotiating mandates on several files in the EU’s next budget, according to four EU officials with knowledge of the discussions — a move that could drag out discussions on the seven-year plan in the chamber.

The challenge would stop the files, which have already been discussed at a committee level, from going straight to talks with national governments. Instead, the mandates would need a plenary vote, opening the door to amendments that could rehash positions committees had already settled.

“The merger of several programs [in several budget proposals] is accompanied by an increasing concentration of allocation authority in the hands of the Commission,” a PfE official told POLITICO. Moreover, most of the PfE’s amendments in the budget have been rejected, they said.

The official added that “several delegations outside of the PfE” have told them they would support the challenge.

title: Croatia: Border Pushbacks of Adults, Children Violate Rights
content:
(Brussels, November 24, 2026) – Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks at the border, including of unaccompanied children and families with young children, despite European Union efforts to end the practice, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. 

The 43-page report, “Doing Europe’s Dirty Work: Ongoing Violent Pushbacks of Migrants from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina,” finds that Croatian authorities routinely engage in pushbacks, often violently. An EU-funded Croatian border monitoring program has had little impact on Croatian police pushbacks. Instead, the EU has increased funding to Croatia for border management without addressing the abuse at the border.

title: ‘It’s just a circus’: Founders clash with notaries over new EU startup law
content:
BRUSSELS — Europe’s plan to help startups compete with Silicon Valley has hit an obstacle in the continent’s most buttoned-up profession: notaries.

Unveiled in March as Europe’s answer to Delaware, the European Commission’s EU Inc. proposal would give new companies a quick way to set up a single EU legal entity, sparing them legal advice and form filling in multiple countries. It would also cut notaries out of key stages in a company’s life cycle, a move that has excited startups and rankled the profession.

“It’s just a circus,” said Mihai Streza, a Berlin-based entrepreneur, who sees hefty notary bills and mandatory in-person appointments as emblematic of what Europe gets wrong about startups.

Pushback by the notaries, however, is now complicating negotiations over the proposed regulation, which would create a single company form allowing startups to register online within 48 hours for €100. EU leaders set the end of this year as the deadline for a political deal, but talks between the Parliament and EU countries have yet to start.

title: Is Artificial Intelligence undermining Freedom of Information?
content:
Guest post by Ben Worthy, David Cuillier, Sheeley Kimball and Suzanne Piotrowski

There is growing concern that Artificial Intelligence is undermining Freedom of Information laws, and that ‘bots’ can be used to ‘flood’ or overwhelm public bodies with requests. In 2023 Wired magazine reported widespread worries that AI bots could flood FOIA officers working in elections in the US, claiming that ‘Election Workers Are Drowning in Records Requests. AI Chatbots Could Make It Worse’. In 2025, the Australian Attorney General proposed a series of restrictions to the Australian Federal FOI law, arguing that ‘technology [is] enabling large volumes of vexatious, abusive and frivolous requests—tying up resources, costing taxpayers money and delaying genuine requests’, and citing claims of ‘FOI bombing’ of particular agencies. The UK government also recently floated the possibility of altering cost limits, again with a hint that AI was driving increased requests. In June 2026 the Scottish Information Commissioner spoke of the ‘potential challenges posed by high‑volumes of AI‑generated requests’ meaning ‘excessive or automated submissions can place considerable strain on organisational resources’.

title: Citing Trafficking Risks, Georgia Plans Total Ban on Surrogacy
content:
Georgia’s ruling party has announced plans to impose a complete ban on surrogacy, framing the move as a campaign against human trafficking and the exploitation of women, even as opposition leaders and fertility doctors accused the government of bowing to the Orthodox Church and threatening families struggling with infertility.

Irakli Kirtskhalia, a lawmaker with the governing Georgian Dream party, said after a meeting of the parliamentary majority that legislation was being drafted to outlaw the practice entirely, though in vitro fertilization would remain legal. Georgia’s surrogacy market has expanded significantly since 2023, Kirtskhalia said, adding that the party had consulted both executive authorities and the Georgian Patriarchate.

“We understand well that banning surrogacy may have a certain economic impact; however, we believe that economic benefits cannot outweigh these risks and ethical issues,” he said.

title: Civil society questions decree that could block access to telecommunications networks in Mozambique
content:
Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression

Originally published on Global Voices Advox

Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025. Photo by Wilson Thole. Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension. The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

title: Statement zum Innenausschuss: AlgorithmWatch warnt vor Fiasko bei KI-Migrationsverwaltungsgesetz
content:
Berlin, 23. November 2026 – Heute berät der Innenausschuss des Deutschen Bundestags über den Entwurf für das KI-Migrationsverwaltungsgesetz (KIMVG). Mit dem Gesetz soll Migrationsbehörden erlaubt werden, KI-Systeme mit Daten aus Visums- und Asylverfahren entwickeln und einsetzen zu dürfen. Bereits vergangene Woche hat AlgorithmWatch mit 36 weiteren Organisationen einen gemeinsamen Appell unterzeichnet und darin konkrete Nachbesserungen in den Bereichen Datenschutz, Evaluation und Transparenz gefordert. Darüber hinaus kritisiert AlgorithmWatch, dass der jetzige Gesetzentwurf zu vielen Behörden erlaubt, beim Einsatz von KI Grundrechte einzuschränken.

Nora Oppermann, Junior Policy Managerin bei AlgorithmWatch, kommentiert:

„Das KIMVG soll einem kaum begrenzten Behördenkreis ermöglichen, mit hochsensiblen Daten eigene KI-Systeme zu entwickeln. Dazu zählen 225 Auslandsvertretungen, 585 kommunale Ausländerbehörden und sämtliche Dienststellen der Polizei. Zwischen touristischen Visa aus Nordamerika und Asylgesuchen von geflüchteten Menschen aus Kriegs- und Krisengebieten wird dabei kein Unterschied gemacht.

title: KeBob
content:
KeBob ist ein KI-basiertes Assistenzsystem des oberösterreichischen Unternehmens KEBA, das für den Einsatz in Bankfoyers entwickelt wurde. Anders als viele KI-Systeme ist es nicht mit einer Cloud verbunden, sondern verarbeitet Informationen lokal und ohne Internetverbindung.

Mithilfe von Kameras erfasst es Situationen in Echtzeit und kann unmittelbar darauf reagieren – etwa bei medizinischen Notfällen oder verdächtigem Verhalten. Auch die Kommunikation mit anderen technischen Systemen ist möglich, um beispielsweise gefährliche Situationen zu vermeiden. Über ein Display mit einem virtuellen Gesicht kann KeBob zudem direkt mit Menschen kommunizieren. 

Das System soll zur Sicherheit beitragen, wirft aber auch Fragen auf: Wie viel Verantwortung lässt sich an künstliche Intelligenz übertragen? Und wie verändert sich das Sicherheitsgefühl, wenn Maschinen das Geschehen im öffentlichen Raum beobachten und bewerten?

title: China Sends Post-Shenzhen Signals to Europe
content:
Europe was left out of the Shenzhen summit, but it wasn’t forgotten, at least in Chinese minds. The state media was quick to send signals that it was thinking of Europe (which in turn has been thinking of targeting Chinese imports).

Xi Jinping’s November 19 appearance with US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, the Russian leader, ended with a statement speaking of peace and co-operation in broad terms.

There was little for diplomats to get their teeth into beyond the images of the US and Chinese leaders standing together, accompanied by the head of a lesser Eurasian power. Europe was absent, and yet Beijing’s messaging suggests it still matters a great deal.

The Chinese party-state is adept at using its coordinated media outlets for coded dispatches in the absence of official position-taking. As initial clues to what comes next, these are worth noting because they serve as a guide to official thinking.

title: Your boss may not be ready to manage AI
content: If you have an office job, chances are you’ve had at least one earnest chat about how AI could streamline your work. Across Europe, 67% of companies are already using generative AI tools, while another 13% plan to do so in the next year. In a 2025 survey more than 70% of Europeans said they felt AI could improve their productivity, while at the same time overwhelmingly supporting safeguards to ensure its responsible use in the workplace. “You can have good principles, but who is responsible for implementing them inside companies?” asked Maxime Legrand, president of the European managers trade union association CEC. “In practice, that’s managers.” Yet much is still unknown about how AI is actually being used in the workplace. That's why his organisation is collaborating with the Technical University of Munich on a study examining how companies are adopting and managing the technology. After speaking with colleagues across Europe, Legrand said many weren't particularly convinced by promises of productivity gains. title: Baltic Sea Region Youth Survey 2027: young people, tell us what matters to you
content:
The Baltic Sea Region Youth Forum (BSRYF) launches a region-wide survey on what matters to young people of age 16-30, and how much they trust politics. The survey is open until 14 December 2026.

How do young people in the Baltic Sea Region see their role in politics and society? The Baltic Sea Region Youth Forum (BSRYF), an independent body of young people supported by the Council of the Baltic Sea States (CBSS), has launched the Baltic Sea Region Youth Survey 2027 to find out.

The survey is open to young people in Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Poland and Sweden and available in all languages. It has four parts:

  • Regional relevance: how much eight topics matter to young people personally and for cooperation in the region, including climate protection, security and resilience, education and economic opportunities, migration, digital transformation, and infrastructure and mobility, and how much say they feel they have on each.
  • Trust in politics: whether young people feel represented, listened to and taken seriously by politicians.
  • Participation in practice: which forms of participation young people use, would consider, and can realistically access.

title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
content:
Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the planned departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

title: Political Prisoner Spotlight: Idris Khattak and the Persecution of Human Rights Defenders in Pakistan
content:
Register 


Human rights defender Idris Khattak spent decades documenting human rights violations, including enforced disappearances, in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province and the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas. In retaliation for this work, he was abducted, disappeared, tortured, and sentenced to 14 years in prison. His ongoing detention highlights how the Pakistani authorities have used extralegal means to silence criticism, deployed national security legislation against perceived opponents, relied on military courts to try civilians, and endangered the lives of political prisoners through mistreatment and medical neglect.

To mark the seven-year anniversary of Idris Khattak’s detention, Freedom House is hosting a virtual event that will discuss the current status of the case, what it reveals about the persecution of human rights defenders in Pakistan more broadly, and how democratic governments and multilateral institutions can respond.

Speakers Include: 

  • Hina Jilani, human rights lawyer and member of The Elders
  • Talia Khattak, daughter of Idris Khattak
  • Laura Rosenberger, executive vice president, Freedom House

title: ”I can do it” – Digitaidot avaavat uusia mahdollisuuksia Zimbabwen nuorille naisille
content:
Milicent Gumbiran, 20, tarina on Zimbabwessa tyypillinen. 

Hänen perheensä ajautui taloudellisiin ongelmiin isän kuoleman jälkeen, ja hän jätti 17-vuotiaana lukion kesken juuri ennen loppukokeita. Viiden lapsen koulumaksut olivat yksinhuoltajaäidille liikaa. 

“Oli tuskallista selviytyä. Joinakin päivinä menimme nukkumaan ilman ruokaa. Se oli hyvin vaikeaa äidilleni ja meille lapsille”, Gumbira kertoo. 

Zimbabwessa koulutuksen loppuun saaminen ei ole itsestäänselvyys, ja vaikka koulutodistuksen saisi käteensä, siirtyminen koulunpenkiltä palkkatyöhön on nuorille vaikeaa tai jopa mahdotonta. Virallisia työpaikkoja on vähän, eivätkä työnhakijoiden taidot usein vastaa työnantajien vaatimuksiin esimerkiksi digitaitojen osalta.  

Zimbabwe on kärsinyt koko 2000-luvun ajan taloudellisesta epävakaudesta sekä lisääntyneestä köyhyydestä. Afrikan kehityspankin mukaan vuonna 2026 noin 40 prosenttia väestöstä elää köyhyysrajan alapuolella (alle kahdella dollarilla päivässä). Zimbabwen tilastokeskuksen mukaan 15–24-vuotiaista noin 48 prosenttia on työvoiman ja koulutuksen ulkopuolella.

title: Interés menguante, desconfianza y polarización: Así se informan los españoles
content:
Los españoles están llamados a votar en las elecciones generales de este domingo. Los sondeos sugieren que Pedro Sánchez, que ha gobernado el país desde 2018, podría perder el poder. Las elecciones son un buen momento para explorar cómo los españoles se informan con la ayuda de más de una década de datos del Digital News Report.

Nuestros datos muestran que las audiencias más jóvenes tienen menos confianza y menos interés en las noticias, y son las más propensas a usar chatbots y redes sociales para informarse. La confianza en la radiotelevisión pública divide profundamente a los españoles, la preocupación por la desinformación en línea está en su punto más alto y muchos critican la cobertura que los medios hacen del clima y la inmigración. A continuación, presentamos nueve hallazgos de nuestro informe.

title: NATO witnesses a surge of airspace violations by Russia as Moscow seeks to test alliance
content:
NATO convened an urgent meeting on Nov. 23, 2026, to discuss the violation of members’ airspace by Russia.

It follows an incident three days earlier in which three objects – believed to be two missiles and a drone – crashed in Poland in what the country’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, described as an “intentional provocation” by Russia. If true, it would be far from the first such testing of the airspace of a NATO country.

Russian aircraft, drones and missiles have violated NATO airspace dozens of times since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. And while individually, many of these incidents appear minor – a drone crash here, a brief fighter incursion there, a missile discovered only after the fact – taken together, I believe the numbers tell a far more troubling story.

To get a full picture of the scale of violations, I conducted a systematic review of Russian airspace violations against NATO members) from 2022 through the end of November.

title: It’s time for scientists to boycott the climate COPs and the IPCC
content:
On Nov. 22, the day after COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya, Turkey, the global average temperature at noon UTC was estimated to be a record-setting 2.36 C above the pre-industrial average.

Climate change is driving up global temperatures. Yet governments could not even agree to name the fossil fuels driving it.

I have been a climate scientist since the late 1980s and have followed every UN climate summit since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. I cannot recall a more embarrassing failure than COP31.

The first draft proposed at least US$120 billion by 2035 to help countries adapt to climate change. By Nov. 19, the figure was gone.

Three years ago in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. The Nov. 16 Antalya draft said so plainly. Yet, the final proposal at COP31 still omitted any mention of fossil fuels. The European Union and small island states were right to reject it.

Given the recent failure, is it time for scientists and activists to boycott COP?

title: Vasemmistopopulistiset demokraattitähdet pyrkivät yhdistämään kansan oligarkiaa vastaan
content:
Yhä useampaa suosittua demokraattipoliitikkoa voi luonnehtia vasemmistopopulistiksi. Vasemmistopopulististen demokraattien suosio heijastaa niin laajaa tyytymättömyyttä vallitsevaan järjestykseen kuin kyllästymistä kahtiajakoja vahvistavaan kulttuurisotimiseen. Mikäli demokraatit onnistuvat populismillaan valjastamaan ihmisten tyytymättömyyden entistäkin tehokkaammin omaksi edukseen, voi heillä vuonna 2029 olla lähes ainutlaatuinen mahdollisuus muuttaa Yhdysvaltoja.

Texasin kuvernööriksi valittu demokraatti Gina Hinojosa totesi ennen 3. marraskuuta pidettyjä välivaaleja ihmisten olevan kyllästyneitä kulttuurisotiin, joista ovat hänen mukaansa hyötyneet ainoastaan teknojätit ja miljardöörit. Demokraattien ”sininen tsunami” osoittaa talouspopulistiksi itseään kutsuvan Hinojosan olleen pitkälti oikeassa, mutta liikaa johtopäätelmiä etenkin presidentti Donald Trumpin epäsuosiota heijastavasta välivaalituloksesta ei pidä vetää.

content:
UN Womenin uuden, 54 maata kattavan Access to Justice for Women Survivors of Violence -tilastokatsauksen mukaan vain joka neljäs (23 %) fyysistä tai seksuaalista väkivaltaa elämänsä aikana kokenut nainen hakee minkäänlaista apua perheeltään, yhteisöltään tai viranomaisilta. title: University Approves Nuclear Weapons Data Center, Township Vows to Fight On
content:
Last week, the University of Michigan’s board of regents approved the construction of a $1.25 billion data center that will power American nuclear weapons research. The regents voted 7 - 1 in a public meeting on November 19 to move forward with the project despite widespread opposition from faculty, staff, and the residents of Ypsilanti Township, Michigan where the data center will operate. A few hours after the vote, the leaders and citizens of the Township gathered to discuss how to stop it.

U of M and Los Alamos National Laboratories (LANL) first announced plans to build what the University then called an “AI research facility” in 2024. title: Bangladesh: Proposed changes to cyber laws risk granting authorities excessive power to police online content
content:
New proposed amendments to Bangladesh’s laws on online speech would give authorities wide-ranging and arbitrary powers to police content and restrict the right to freedom of expression, Amnesty International said today.

The new draft Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, 2026 would grant government agencies overly broad powers to remove, block, or relocate any online content deemed to fall within a range of broadly defined categories that do not constitute legitimate reasons to restrict the right to freedom of expression under international human rights law. These include content that “undermines” the integrity, dignity […] of the country”, or content that is “likely to create religious or communal hatred”. The lowering of the threshold for removal or blocking to content which ‘is likely to’ undermine security or create religious or communal hatred is vague and speculative.

title: We Need a Third Reconstruction: Bishop William Barber Pushes Democrats to Take Action After Midterms
content:
With Democrats preparing to take control of both houses of Congress in January, Bishop William Barber of Repairers of the Breach argues the coalition that delivered the Democrats their midterm victories must now hold the incoming Congress accountable and keep organizing from the ground up. He and other faith leaders are calling on members of the incoming Congress to join them outside the U.S. Capitol next month to sign “A Pledge for Moral Defiance” — a commitment to pass legislation that addresses the needs of poor and working people and other vulnerable communities. Barber is pushing for what he describes as a Third Reconstruction: a sweeping moral and political agenda that includes a living wage, universal healthcare, protecting voting rights, affordable housing, environmental justice and comprehensive immigration reform.

“This was a vote not for Democrats,” says Barber. “It was a vote to say, 'Will you use policy to answer the pain that we are experiencing in this country at this particular moment?'”

title: Ei pirstaloitumiselle – Etla ehdottaa uuden EU-rahoituksen kohdentamista tekoälyinfraan, soteen ja puolustukseen
content:
Euroopan unionin uusi rahoituskehys voisi tarjota Suomelle liki viiden miljardin euron potin, kun mukaan lasketaan kansallinen vastinrahoitus. Etlan tuoreen muistion mukaan uusi rahoituskehys avaa myös Suomelle tilaisuuden uudistua. Rahoitus tulisi keskittää sellaisiin investointeihin ja uudistuksiin, jotka uhkaavat muuten jäädä toteuttamatta julkisen talouden tiukassa tilanteessa. Mahdollisia kohteita ovat Etlan mukaan muun muassa julkisen sektorin tekoäly- ja datainfrastruktuuri, sote-uudistus, puhdas teollisuus sekä puolustus ja varautuminen. Sääntöjen luoma liikkumavara ei muuta julkisen talouden budjettirajoitteita. Kyseessä ei ole ilmainen raha vaan julkisen rahoituksen tulee perustua tunnistettavaan tarpeeseen.

Euroopan komission ehdotus unionin vuosien 2028–2034 monivuotiseksi rahoituskehykseksi muuttaisi toteutuessaan EU-rahan käyttöä merkittävästi nykyisestä. Korvamerkittyä rahoitusta olisi aiempaa vähemmän, mutta jäsenvaltioiden harkintaan jäävää rahoitusta puolestaan enemmän. Suomelle voisi kohdistua arviolta 4,5–5,5 miljardia euroa, kun mukaan luetaan myös kansallinen vastinrahoitus.

title: COP31 Failed Climate-Displaced Communities
content:
Leaving the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, I can’t shake the disconnect between the reality of entire communities losing their homes to rising seas and some governments’ apathy and obstruction of the process. The conference ended without consensus on the proposed Antalya Pact—the overarching political agreement for the COP31 climate summit.

I am still in awe of Francis, a community leader from Solomon Islands who traveled to Antalya to share his story. “Walande… the birthplace written in my passport, no longer exists,” he told a hushed room. “It is submerged beneath the waves.” His words moved the high-level event’s moderator to tears.

title: Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece
content:
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch, Girl with a Pearl Earring, and The Garden of Earthly Delights. But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece, also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece, seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

title: More than 99 per cent of Gaza shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israel’s military assault
content:
Israel's destruction of Gaza through the extensive use of explosive and incendiary weapons has made air, soil and water dangerous to Palestinians now and for decades to come, with indicators of toxic contamination across almost the entirety of the Strip. 

New analyses in a report released by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) today, has found that Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination risks across Gaza, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants threatening the environmental life support systems that people in Gaza depend upon for survival.

“Environmental War Crimes: How Israel’s military assault has turned Gaza into a toxic wasteland, threatening human survival” found that the scale and intensity of the Israeli military’s onslaught has affected approximately 78 per cent of Gaza’s land area, with the report’s spatial analysis identifying indicators of potential contamination across more than 99 per cent of the territory; highlighting the scale and near-total geographical spread of pollution risks.

title: Miten kehitysyhteistyö eroaa hätäavusta?
content:
Kehitysyhteistyö eroaa hätäavusta siinä, että sen tavoitteena ei ole tarjota tilapäistä helpotusta vaan rakentaa pysyviä rakenteita, jotka mahdollistavat yhteisöjen oman kehityksen. Hätäapu eli humanitaarinen apu vastaa välittömään tarpeeseen, kun taas kehitysyhteistyö kysyy, miksi tuo tarve on olemassa ja miten se poistetaan pysyvästi. Alla käymme läpi kehitysyhteistyön keskeisimmät kysymykset yksityishenkilöiden ja yritysten näkökulmasta.

Kehitysyhteistyö on pitkäjänteistä toimintaa, jossa tuetaan haavoittuvien yhteisöjen omia voimavaroja koulutuksen, toimeentulon ja rauhan rakentamisen kautta. Se ei ole avun antamista ulkoapäin vaan kumppanuutta, jossa paikalliset yhteisöt ovat aktiivisia toimijoita omassa kehityksessään.

Käytännössä kehitysyhteistyö voi tarkoittaa esimerkiksi sitä, että konflikteista kärsivillä alueilla varmistetaan lasten mahdollisuus käydä koulua, tuetaan paikallisia yrittäjiä luomaan kestävä toimeentulo tai vahvistetaan yhteisöjen kykyä ratkaista konflikteja rauhanomaisesti. Toiminta suunnitellaan yhdessä paikallisten kumppanien kanssa, jotta tulokset vastaavat todellisiin tarpeisiin eivätkä ulkopuolisten oletuksiin.

CDIF progress: new profiles and roadmap coming soon!
content:
Developments on the Cross-Domain Interoperability Framework (CDIF) have been moving rapidly since the release of version 1.1 and the launch of the CDIF4EOSC project in June 2026. Work has been focused on both immediate- and longer-term objectives, in a variety of areas. Chief among these are the new profiles under development, a long-running process which is now bearing fruit. Efforts to support the further development of cross-domain metadata models at W3C are on-going, and there are developments in terms of tools, maintenance, and training. The recent workshop ‘Optimising Metadata Structures for Alignments with Standard Models at the Point of Use’ at the Leibniz Foundation’s Schloss Dagstuhl in Wadern, Germany saw many of these activities come to a head.

New Profiles: Provenance, Access Rights and DCAT-Syntax for Core and Discovery Profiles

title: Op-ed | Climate Security Requires Scientific Diplomacy Beyond Geopolitical Tensions
content:
Drawing on fifteen years of experience working at the intersection of science and diplomacy, including a long-running scientific collaboration with North Korea, James Hammond explores the diplomatic and soft-power value of scientific partnerships, the risks posed by their disruption and why protecting them should be considered a national and international security priority.

Climate change is increasingly recognised as a national security threat. Recent statements by the Prime Minister at COP31[1] in Türkiye and the Foreign Secretary at the UN General Assembly[2], together with the appointment of Dame Madeline Alessandri as the world’s first Special Representative for Climate Security, reflect that growing awareness. Yet one aspect receives far less attention: climate security depends upon international scientific collaboration. As geopolitical tensions rise and scientific ties come under increasing pressure, protecting those collaborations should itself be viewed as a security imperative.

title: Blogi: Vahva Eurooppa keskittyy olennaiseen
content:
Euroopan unionin budjetista keskusteltaessa huomio kiinnittyy helposti yhteen kysymykseen: kuinka suuri budjetin pitäisi olla? Olennaisempi kysymys on kuitenkin se, mitä yhteisillä euroilla saadaan aikaan.

Eurooppa elää perusteellisesti muuttuneessa maailmassa. Venäjän hyökkäyssota on palauttanut turvallisuuden politiikan keskiöön. Kansainvälinen kilpailu teknologiasta, investoinneista ja raaka-aineista kiristyy. Samalla meidän on vahvistettava Euroopan taloutta, huolehdittava ulkorajojemme turvallisuudesta ja tuettava Ukrainaa pitkäjänteisesti.

Näihin haasteisiin yksikään jäsenmaa ei pysty vastaamaan yksin. Siksi tarvitsemme Euroopan unionia ja yhteistä eurooppalaista budjettia.

EU-myönteisyys ei kuitenkaan tarkoita sitä, että jokainen budjetin kasvattamista koskeva esitys pitäisi hyväksyä. Todellista eurooppalaista vastuunkantoa on huolehtia siitä, että yhteiset varat käytetään tavoitteisiin, joissa yhteistyö tuottaa enemmän vaikuttavuutta kuin jäsenmaiden toiminta erikseen.

title: Grant OPUS LAP dla prof. Bartosza Pielińskiego na badania nad samoregulacją AI w społecznościach otwartych zasobów cyfrowych
content:
Z przyjemnością informujemy, że dr hab. Bartosz Pieliński, prof. UW, członek naszej Katedry UNESCO, otrzymał finansowanie w prestiżowym konkursie OPUS 30 LAP/Weave Narodowego Centrum Nauki (NCN). Jego projekt pt. „Zmiana reguł, norm i strategii związanych ze wspólnymi zasobami otwartego oprogramowania i otwartej treści w wyniku pojawienia się dużych modeli językowych” (Changing Rules, Norms and Strategies of the Open Source and Open Content Commons Following the Emergence of Large Language Models) poświęcony jest temu, w jaki sposób społeczności internetowe samodzielnie wypracowują zasady korzystania z narzędzi sztucznej inteligencji.

Projekt koncentruje się na dwóch typach społeczności, na które rozwój generatywnej sztucznej inteligencji wywiera szczególnie istotny wpływ: społecznościach rozwijających otwarte oprogramowanie (open source) oraz tworzących otwarte zasoby treści (open content). Badania obejmą m.in. społeczności skupione wokół rozwoju Linuksa i Wikipedii, analizując, jak reagują one na upowszechnienie narzędzi opartych na dużych modelach językowych (LLM).

title: Ministeri Tavio vierailee Etelä-Afrikassa
content:
Ulkomaankauppa- ja kehitysministeri Ville Tavio tekee vienninedistämisvierailun Etelä-Afrikkaan 23.–26. marraskuuta yhdessä yritysvaltuuskunnan kanssa. Team Finland -matkan ohjelmaan sisältyy korkean tason tapaamisia ja yritystapahtumia. Matkan tavoitteena on vahvistaa Suomen ja Etelä-Afrikan kaupallistaloudellisia suhteita.

Ulkomaankauppa- ja kehitysministeri Ville Tavion vienninedistämismatkan yritysdelegaatiossa on mukana seitsemän yritystä, jotka edustavat pääasiassa kaivos-, kiertotalous- ja digitalisaatiosektoreita. Delegaatiossa ovat mukana myös Suomen itsenäisyyden juhlarahasto Sitra ja rahoitusyhtiö Finnvera.  

Ministeri Tavio tapaa vierailunsa aikana Etelä-Afrikan hallinnon korkeita edustajia. Keskusteluissa keskitytään maiden välisten kauppa- ja taloussuhteiden vahvistamiseen. Lisäksi vierailun aikana tutustutaan muun muassa Nokian paikallisiin toimintoihin ja Pretorian yliopiston puuteknologian laboratorioon. Ministeri vierailee myös Sibanye-Stillwaterin platinakaivoksella.

Matkan ohjelmaan sisältyy kaksi yritysseminaaria.

title: Iraq’s Oil Minister Denies Ouster Rumors as Najaf Smuggling Scandal Widens
content:
Iraq’s Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair al-Abadi on Monday denied media reports  that prime minister Ali Al Zaidi was considering dismissing him following the discovery of possible oil smuggling operations in the Iraqi province of Najaf this weekend. 

"The issue of resignation is completely unfounded," al-Abadi said in a statement, adding that he fully supports the government’s anti-corruption efforts.

Al-Abadi’s reaction came after Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council on Saturday said a court issued arrest warrants against the head of the Energy Committee at the Najaf Provincial Council and his brother after an investigating judge conducted a field inspection in a plot of land belonging to the siblings.

The judge found “encroachment on one of the oil pipelines in the Najaf Governorate,” the statement said, adding that the two men “had previously dug a trench surrounding the plot of land on all sides, hindering access and preventing people from observing the activities taking place there.”

title: Durchleuchtet – Anatomie eines Roboters
content:
Was steckt eigentlich in einem humanoiden Roboter? Um das herauszufinden, muss er nicht auseinandergenommen werden. Für dieses Projekt wurde der Roboter Oli im Kepler Universitätsklinikum einer Computertomographie (CT) unterzogen.

Die Aufnahmen machen sein Inneres sichtbar und geben Einblick in eine technische Blackbox, die normalerweise verborgen bleibt. Dabei zeigt sich: Auch wenn Oli äußerlich an den menschlichen Körper erinnert, besteht sein Innenleben aus Motoren, Kabeln und elektronischen Bauteilen. Seine Konstruktion orientiert sich in ihrer Form am menschlichen Körper, folgt im Inneren aber ganz eigenen Prinzipien. 

Credit:
Prof. Franz Fellner, Daniel Schneeweiß, Kepler Universitätsklinikum (KUK) Linz

title: Working for nothing
content: How would you feel if I told you that, from today, you would no longer be paid for your work until the end of the year? For millions of women, this is effectively what the gender pay gap amounts to. Every year, the French feminist movement Les Glorieuses turns the gender pay gap into a date marking when women in effect start working for free. This year, the campaign celebrates its 10th anniversary. In France, that moment fell on 19 November at 10.51 – hence its #19Novembre10h51 movement. But what if we applied the same calculation across the EU? According to Eurostat, women in the EU earned, on average, 11.1% less per hour than men in 2024. Applying Les Glorieuses’ methodology, this translates into approximately 28 unpaid working days. On that basis, the EU's symbolic date would fall on 23 November 09.12. But why does the gender pay gap persist? Among other reasons, women remain overrepresented in lower-paid sectors, take on a greater share of unpaid care work – which can lead to more part-time employment – and have fewer opportunities to progress into senior roles. title: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
content: About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.

title: OPINION: Who Gets to Design the Future of Food Systems?
content:
The future of food systems should be shaped with the people whose lives depend on them.

By Neena Joshi*

KATHMANDU, Nepal | 23 November 2026 (IDN) — Tara Devi, a smallholder farmer from Muzaffarpur, Bihar, India, understands what it takes to make a farming household more resilient. As a Community Agro-Vet Entrepreneur (CAVE), she provides livestock health services and advice to 700–800 families in her community. Her work connects smallholder farmers with the knowledge and services they need to protect their livestock, improve productivity and strengthen their livelihoods.

But Tara’s experience also raises a bigger question about the future of food systems. Who gets to shape the solutions designed to transform them?

The development community has become increasingly sophisticated at designing solutions for a more resilient and sustainable food system. Blended finance, catalytic capital, climate finance, technology, regenerative agriculture and new investment models are giving us powerful tools to address complex challenges. Yet, for all our sophistication, we still too often design for communities rather than with them.

The future of food systems should be shaped with the people whose lives depend on them.

title: Shrinking interest and divided trust: How Spaniards get their news
content:
Spaniards will soon head to the polls for a snap general election on 29 November. The latest polls suggest the vote is an uphill battle for the country’s centre-left prime minister. After being in power since 2018, Pedro Sánchez now risks being ousted by a right-wing government. The election is a good moment to explore how Spaniards get their news with the help of more than a decade of survey data from our Digital News Report. 

Our surveys show news use in Spain is divided across age groups, with younger audiences more critical, less interested and more likely to use AI chatbots and social media for news than older age groups. Both interest and trust have plummeted in the past decade, with trust in the public broadcaster deeply polarised along political lines. Many Spaniards are critical of climate and immigration coverage, and concerns about online misinformation are at their peak. Here are nine findings from our research.

title: Poland continues to support Ukraine militarily, but economic relations are strained
content:
Poland recently announced it would transfer two MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in exchange for anti-drone technology. The agreement comes at a time when Russian drones and missiles are wandering into Polish airspace on a regular basis.

The latest incursion occurred on November 20. Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Polish airspace was violated three times during Russian attacks on Ukraine that day. The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, called the incidents “intentional provocation” by Russia.

Poland has been a staunch ally of Ukraine since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. It has already transferred 14 MiG-29s to Ukraine, as part of a plan to move Kyiv away from older Russian fighters towards western jets. Poland has also provided over €4.4 billion (£3.7 billion) in aid, and has donated over 350 tanks and 250 infantry fighting vehicles to Ukraine.

title: PNG’s parliament is voting on ratifying Bougainville independence. A ‘no’ won’t be the end of the story
content:
After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process.

In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result.

A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving.

Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track.

Bougainville was named by French navigator Louis Antoine de Bougainville in the 18th century, and colonialism has shaped its history ever since. In 1899, it was incorporated into German New Guinea, while the neighbouring Solomon Islands became a British protectorate.
